segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Court

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over this series we are going to move through Dickens's sprawling, magnificent masterpiece — chapter by chapter, passage by passage, character by character.
Bleak House is a novel about fog — literal and figurative — about a court case that devours lives, and about a young woman who tells half the story with disarming honesty.
To do it justice, I've brought three people who love it in very different ways.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — always looking for the genius of the construction.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive, and he hears this prose the way it was meant to be heard — as performance, as voice, as comic and tragic theatre.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — someone who knows exactly where the novel will break your heart, and when it earns a laugh.
Welcome, all three of you.
Let's begin where Dickens begins — with fog.
The fog is the most famous opening gambit in Victorian fiction, and it earns that reputation completely.
Dickens doesn't just describe fog — he makes it the novel's governing intelligence.
It seeps into everything — the law, the aristocracy, Chancery itself.
What I find structurally thrilling is that the fog arrives before any character does.
The environment is the argument — before we meet a single human soul, Dickens has told us what kind of world this is.
And then Chancery emerges from the fog like something that has always been there and always will be — which is precisely the horror.
Oliver, you've spoken these opening pages aloud more times than most people have read them silently.
What do they feel like from the inside — from the performer's position?
They feel like a dare.
Dickens opens with no character, no plot, no dialogue — just this insistent, almost hypnotic accumulation of fog and mud and ancient legal obstruction.
As a performer, you have to trust that the reader — or the listener — will follow you into that atmosphere before they know why.
Now, Tulkinghorn emerges from that world — he is, in some ways, its perfect creature.
Dickens gives us his appearance before his actions, and the description is a masterpiece of compressed malevolence.
"Rustily drest, with his spectacles in his hand, and their very case worn threadbare. In manner, close and dry. In voice, husky and low. In face, watchful behind a blind."
That phrase — watchful behind a blind — is as good a three-word character portrait as exists in English fiction.
And then Dickens twists the knife with a line of perfect irony.
"The peerage may have warmer worshippers and faithfuller believers than Mr. Tulkinghorn, after all, if everything were known."
That final clause — if everything were known — hangs over the entire novel like a question that refuses to be answered.
What Oliver is describing is Dickens's peculiar genius for the loaded withholding — he gives you everything and nothing simultaneously.
Tulkinghorn never explains himself, never confides, never slips — and that absence of interiority is itself terrifying.
Compare him to Esther, who over-explains, who apologises for her own perceptions — the contrast is almost architectural.
The dual narration isn't just a structural flourish — it's a moral argument about who gets to know what, and at what cost.
And yet when I think about what keeps me coming back to this novel, it isn't the architecture — though Eleanor is right that it's extraordinary.
It's the moments when a character surprises you with their warmth — when the human breaks through all that fog.
There's a moment with Richard — poor, doomed Richard Carstone — that I find almost unbearably tender.
He sees Woodcourt arrive unexpectedly, and he cries out with this sudden, boyish delight.
"Woodcourt, my dear fellow — you come upon my vision like a ghost."
It's a comic line — but read it in context, and the word ghost turns cold.
Richard is haunted already — by Chancery, by his own squandered promise.
Dickens lets a throwaway phrase carry the whole tragedy of a character.
Caroline has hit on something that I think is the secret of the novel's power — Dickens can make a joke and a lament from the same words.
As a performer, those moments are the most demanding — you have to hold both registers at once.
And Tulkinghorn, by contrast, operates in a register that's entirely his own — pure menace dressed as social nicety.
There's a scene where he examines Lady Dedlock's portrait and delivers what sounds almost like a drawing-room observation.
"Who is this? 'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character."
The cruelty there is almost invisible — it's wrapped in the language of connoisseurship.
He's not speaking about a painting — he's speaking directly at Lady Dedlock, and she knows it, and so does every reader in the room.
What a way to begin — fog, menace, and already the faint sound of a life unravelling.
In our next segment, we're going to go deeper into the machinery of Chancery and what it does to the people trapped inside it.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Machinery of Chancery: Richard's First Steps

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, where we're working our way through Dickens's great novel of fog, law, and the slow ruin of everything it touches.
Today we're focusing on the machinery of Chancery — how it draws people in, how it shapes them, and what it costs.
Richard Carstone's first steps toward ruin are our subject, and we'll be moving through some extraordinary writing about power, secrecy, and the quiet devastation of false hope.
With me today — Eleanor Hartley, who teaches creative writing and thinks about how Dickens constructs his effects with a novelist's eye.
Oliver Trevelyan, actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any living person — which means he hears this prose in a way most of us simply can't.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and lifelong Dickens reader who has lived with Bleak House across five complete re-readings.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with a small, comic scene that seems almost beside the point.
Esther watching Charley struggle with her copy-book — what does Dickens give us there, and why does it matter?
It's a passage that could read as pure charm — Esther peeping over Charley's shoulder, the comedy of a pen that behaves like a 'saddle-donkey.'
But Dickens is doing something much more precise here — he's constructing a tiny emblem of the whole novel's concern with writing, documents, and what hands can and cannot do.
The simile is where the passage earns its keep.
Listen to how he puts it:
"every pen appeared to become perversely animated, and to go wrong and crooked, and to stop, and splash, and sidle into corners like a saddle-donkey."
The accumulation of verbs — wrong, crooked, stop, splash, sidle — that's not decoration; that's comic rhythm built out of grammar itself.
And then that gorgeous paradox: 'what old letters Charley's young hand had made, they so wrinkled and shrivelled and tottering, it so plump and round.'
That contrast — the ancient, decrepit text produced by the young, capable hand — is Dickens in miniature.
It's comic, yes, but it's also the novel's central anxiety: that the legal documents shaping these young lives are monstrous old things, written in a hand no one living chose.
I love that reading, Eleanor, because it rescues the passage from being merely delightful.
Though I'd argue being delightful is itself doing serious work in this novel.
Dickens earned your trust with the comedy so that when he turns the knife, you feel it twice as sharp.
Speaking of turning the knife — Tulkinghorn.
There's a description of him that I've read aloud probably a hundred times and it still gives me a slight chill.
It goes like this:
"He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields."
What Dickens captures is the terrifying quality of a man for whom no place is quite real — because all places are merely venues for his business.
He doesn't travel — he transfers. Like a document moving between files.
And that verb 'melted' at the end — 'he melts into his own square' — is perfect.
Solid men don't melt. Only secrets do.
What strikes me about Tulkinghorn — and this is something I felt viscerally on my first reading — is that Dickens gives him an even deeper mystery than his function.
It's not just that he keeps secrets. It's that his own inner life is the most impenetrable secret of all.
There's a passage I return to every time because Dickens doesn't resolve it — he just holds the question open, and that is the horror.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret.
He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
He is his own client. That stopped me cold the first time I read it.
He has professionalized his own soul. Whatever he actually feels — if he feels anything — is filed away, inaccessible, subject to attorney-client privilege with himself.
Caroline, that's exactly right — and it connects to what Dickens does with the whole ruling class in this novel, which is show how they are managed even as they believe themselves to be managing.
There's that extraordinary satirical passage about Lady Dedlock — and what's genius about it is that the satire is structural, not just tonal.
She believes herself an inscrutable Being, utterly beyond the calculation of ordinary mortals.
Meanwhile every dim little star in her orbit — maid, opera manager, jeweller — has her mapped to the millimetre.
And then Dickens drops in this astonishing simile — Gulliver and the Lilliputian fleet.
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput"
The grandeur is entirely ironic — 'majestic Lilliput' — but it's also genuinely funny as a physical image.
The great and powerful are tiny boats, dragged off by their own vanity and their dressmakers' careful study of their worst impulses.
And Mr. Sladdery — the librarian — gets his own little aria in that passage, and I cannot read it without grinning.
'My high connexion, sir' — three times, with that beautiful little sting at the end that he is an honest man and does not exaggerate at all.
Dickens understood that the most effective comic form is the one that pretends to be straight-faced about its own absurdity.
But here's what I find most remarkable about this section of the novel — and it ties back to Richard.
All these forces — Tulkinghorn, the fashionable world, Chancery itself — operate on exactly the same principle as Lady Dedlock's dressmakers.
They study your weaknesses. They hit you in your weakest place. And they are endlessly patient.
And Richard's weakest place is hope.
Not greed, not laziness — hope. That's what makes his destruction so painful.
Esther's narration in the passage about Woodcourt's visit to Symond's Inn is very carefully calibrated — Dickens shows us Esther working out something she doesn't quite want to know.
The line she arrives at is devastating in its quietness.
"It revived a fear I had had before that my dear girl's little property would be absorbed by Mr. Vholes and that Richard's justification to himself would be sincerely this."
'Sincerely this.' Esther isn't accusing Richard of cynicism.
She's saying something much worse — that he genuinely believes the lie he's telling himself. That the self-deception is complete.
Ada's money will go to Vholes, and Richard will feel, sincerely, that it was in service of the case that was going to save them both.
The dual narration is doing something crucial there that I want to flag.
Esther is telling us about Woodcourt telling her about his visit — we're three removes from the event itself.
That distance is not evasion — it's precision. It's Dickens showing us how bad news travels through networks of care.
Woodcourt sees it; he brings it to Esther; Esther has to absorb it while simultaneously tending to Caddy.
And Dickens marks that burden with a single, precise phrase: 'the shade was still between me and my darling.'
"the shade was still between me and my darling"
That word 'shade' carries so much — estrangement, foreknowledge, grief not yet arrived but already darkening the light.
What comes through in all three of these passages is how Dickens shows power operating — through patience, through self-deception, through the slow accumulation of small concessions.
Richard doesn't fall — he drifts, sincerely, toward the thing that will consume him.
And Chancery, like Tulkinghorn, simply waits.
We'll be back after the break to look at how that drift accelerates — and what it costs the people who love Richard most.

segments.title: Jo's Footprints: Dickens on Social Injustice

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart sentence by sentence to see how it works — and why it still matters.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at something close to the heart of the novel: the way Dickens threads individual lives together through accident, fate, and the quiet persistence of compassion.
With me today are three exceptional guides to this extraordinary book.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for Dickens's structural brilliance is, frankly, unmatched.
She sees the architecture beneath the emotion, and she makes you see it too.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than any living actor, and he comes to the text first as a performer — hearing the rhythms, the comic timing, the moments written for the voice.
He is, himself, perpetually quotable.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since.
She reads with her whole self — alert to what's funny, what's devastating, what makes you stop and re-read a sentence in the dark.
Today we begin with Jo — the crossing-sweeper, the boy who knows nothing — and with the strange web of lives that Dickens weaves around him.
What strikes me every time I come back to the Jo chapters — and I've read them aloud more times than I can count — is how Dickens refuses to let the boy be merely a symbol.
Jo is used as a symbol, yes — of ignorance, of exclusion, of institutional failure — but the prose keeps insisting on his physical particularity.
And then you get a passage like this one, where Dickens gathers the people around Jo's sickbed and simply shows you what connection looks like.
"How strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast in the web of very different lives."
That word — entangled — is doing tremendous work.
It's not a neat design, not providence — it's a tangle, something accidental, almost ungainly.
And yet out of that tangle comes this extraordinary gathering of care.
What I find so moving in that scene is the detail of Phil Squod — this extraordinary minor figure with his smoky gunpowder face — who is simultaneously working at his armourer's table and nursing Jo.
Dickens doesn't pause the world for the dying boy.
Life goes on at the little table in the corner, and the care is folded into the ordinary.
And then there's that line about George, the trooper — Dickens writes of his "superfluity of life and strength" seeming to shed vigour down upon Jo.
"Seeming to shed down temporary vigour upon Jo, who never fails to speak more robustly in answer to his cheerful words."
Temporary.
Dickens chooses that word deliberately — the vigour is borrowed, not given, and it won't last.
Both of you are pointing at something structural, even if you're not calling it that — which is Dickens's technique of moral illumination through juxtaposition.
He places the very large — fate, society, injustice — inside the very small: one boy, one smoky corner, one eyebrow raised in encouragement.
But what I want to hold up against this is a passage that seems entirely different in register — earlier in the novel, and comic rather than tragic.
It's Jarndyce introducing Boythorn — and it's one of the great character portraits in English comic fiction.
Listen to how Jarndyce describes him — the structure of the sentences performs the very excess they're describing.
"He is always in extremes, perpetually in the superlative degree.
In his condemnation he is all ferocity."
All ferocity — not some, not considerable — all.
The superlative degree isn't just Boythorn's quality — it's the syntactic key to how Dickens writes the whole character.
Eleanor, from a performer's perspective, that Boythorn passage is a gift — but it's a gift with a trap inside.
You can go too big.
The comic momentum is already in the writing — Dickens has done your work for you — and if you try to amplify it further you capsize.
What saves the comedy — and this is what makes Jarndyce such a magnificent narrator voice — is the punchline that arrives almost as an aside.
"Our friendship began in his knocking two of my head tyrant's teeth out — he says six — before breakfast."
He says six.
Two words, parenthetical, and the whole character is there — the magnificent extravagance, the cheerful unreliability about quantities.
And before breakfast — the best comic detail in the sentence, left till last, completely unnecessary, utterly essential.
The comedy earns the tenderness later, doesn't it.
We love Boythorn partly because Jarndyce loves him with such unguarded warmth — and that warmth is what we carry forward when the novel gets dark.
I think that's what Dickens understood better than almost any novelist — that you have to make people laugh before you can make them grieve.
And the Mrs. Rouncewell passage shows him doing the reverse — taking a moment of almost unbearable feeling and containing it in perfect stillness.
There's a sentence there I've never been able to read without stopping.
"Only her fluttering hands give utterance to her emotions.
But they are very eloquent, very, very eloquent."
That repetition — very, very — is so simple it should be banal.
Instead it breaks your heart.
What Dickens is doing there is surrendering the narrator's authority deliberately.
He has an omniscient narrator who could tell us exactly what Mrs. Rouncewell feels.
Instead he routes the emotion through the hands — through gesture, not language — and then offers us Mrs. Bagnet as witness.
The passage builds to something almost overwhelming — and then Dickens names every emotion at once, one after another.
"They speak of gratitude, of joy, of grief, of hope; of inextinguishable affection, cherished with no return since this stalwart man was a stripling."
Cherished with no return.
The whole history of maternal love estranged — decades of separation, the prodigal son who didn't come home — compressed into four words.
And then Mrs. Bagnet's tears run — not fall, not flow — run glistening down her sun-brown face.
The physical precision is what makes it true.
What I'm hearing across all of this is how consistently Dickens anchors his largest themes in bodily, specific, concrete detail.
The fluttering hands, the smoky face, the teeth knocked out before breakfast — the grand indictment is always carried by the small particular.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at how that technique plays out in Esther's narration — the other voice of this novel, and in some ways its moral centre.

segments.title: Secrets in the Parlour: Lady Dedlock's Buried Past

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great labyrinthine masterpiece apart, passage by passage, to see how it works and why it endures.
Today we're deep inside one of the novel's most compelling mysteries: Lady Dedlock, her buried past, and the extraordinary composure with which she carries it.
With me today are three guests who know this novel with an intimacy that is, frankly, enviable.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for structural craft — the architecture beneath the prose — is second to none.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive, and he hears the rhythms of this novel in ways most of us simply miss.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first encountered Bleak House as a teenager and has re-read it five times — each time, she tells me, finding new reasons to be stopped in her tracks.
Let's begin at the beginning — or rather, at Lincolnshire, which is where Dickens chooses to place Lady Dedlock and her secrets first.
What strikes me every time I read that Lincolnshire passage is how thoroughly Dickens weaponises the weather.
It isn't simply atmosphere — it's moral atmosphere.
The landscape is literally saturated with suppression — things that cannot fall properly, cannot crack, cannot sound.
And then he gives us this.
"The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink."
Lead-coloured and Indian ink — those aren't simply colours, they're the colours of documents, of legal records, of things written down and buried.
And she looks out of those windows every day.
She cannot not see it.
That colour pairing is extraordinary when you look at it closely.
Dickens is essentially showing us Lady Dedlock's visual field as a series of smothered contrasts — a view that changes but never brightens.
But what I keep returning to is the structural decision to plant the Ghost's Walk here, in this very first portrait of her place.
We hear it before we understand it — the dripping onto the flagged pavement, all night long.
That's a Dickens technique I find almost unbearably clever: install the omen, let it sit, let the reader carry it forward without knowing why.
And then — and this is what Caroline is pointing at — the scene at the keeper's lodge.
Lady Dedlock, who is childless — Dickens inserts that word in parentheses, almost casually — sees a woman, a child, a man coming through the gate.
A complete family unit.
And she is, as Dickens puts it, "put quite out of temper."
That phrase — "put quite out of temper" — is doing such extraordinary work.
Because we know, by this point, that Lady Dedlock is not a woman who is put out of temper by anything — that is her defining characteristic.
Tulkinghorn will later say she is boredom itself.
And yet a child running through the rain cracks something in her.
As a performer, when I reach that line, I have to slow right down.
Because Dickens is doing something very quiet there — so quiet you could miss it entirely.
He covers the grief with the social report — she says she has been "bored to death" — and the quotation marks around that phrase carry the entire weight of the irony.
That irony is, of course, the key to her whole performance of self — the composed surface over the turbulent interior.
Eleanor, Dickens shows us Lady Dedlock at the absolute height of her social dominance even as the ground is shifting beneath her.
How does he hold those two things together?
It's one of his most brilliant architectural moves in the whole novel.
Look at the chapter that opens with her in society — where she is at her most apparently formidable.
Dickens writes:
"From the shining heights she has scaled and taken, she is never absent."
"Scaled and taken" — that's military language.
She hasn't simply arrived in society — she has conquered it, and she holds that position by sheer force of will.
And then comes the devastating qualification: though the belief she reposed in herself has been beaten down.
She is more haughty, they say.
More handsome.
Dickens understands that when a person is collapsing internally, the external performance often becomes more intense, more perfectly maintained — not less.
And that tension — between performance and collapse — is what makes the chapter with Tulkinghorn so unbearable to read.
There's a moment after they have spoken — or rather, after Tulkinghorn has delivered his threat — where Dickens simply describes what she does.
She has eaten no dinner.
But she has poured out water with a steady hand.
She reclines in her chair, shading her face.
That steady hand — it's one of the most precise details in the novel.
Because we know what it costs.
And then Tulkinghorn observes her.
"This woman," thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view, "is a study."
A study.
He reduces her to an object of intellectual curiosity — and the word "object" is doing double duty, because he is also physically closing up her view.
He stands between her and the light — literally.
That passage is the one I find hardest to read aloud, and I mean that as the highest compliment to Dickens.
Because "is a study" has to land with absolute weight — and absolutely no drama.
Any inflection in the wrong direction and you've made it melodrama.
What I try to find in Tulkinghorn's voice is a kind of administrative satisfaction — the satisfaction of a man filing something away.
And Lady Dedlock — she's the hardest character Dickens ever wrote for the voice.
She almost never speaks, and when she does, the words are minimal.
The performance of her is almost entirely in what Dickens tells us she doesn't say, doesn't show, doesn't allow herself.
And yet the secrets do surface — in the most alarming ways.
Caroline, the scene where Esther watches a figure approaching through the wood — Lady Dedlock coming toward her with unusual haste — it's one of the novel's great moments of revelation.
What makes it work so powerfully on the page?
It works because it's narrated by Esther, and Esther doesn't know what she's looking at.
And we — the reader — are slightly ahead of her, which is almost unbearable.
Dickens has Esther narrate the approach with this slow, dawning recognition — the figure is first just a figure, then a woman's, then a lady's.
And then:
"By little and little it revealed itself to be a woman's — a lady's — Lady Dedlock's."
Those dashes — they're not decoration, they're the rhythm of recognition arriving, one stage at a time.
And then Esther notices something wrong — something unprecedented.
Lady Dedlock is walking quickly.
For a character defined by her stillness, by her glacial composure, to be moving toward someone with urgency — that single detail does everything.
And it is, of course, the Ghost's Walk that Esther has been looking at as she waits.
Dickens plants that detail with surgical precision — Esther is contemplating the haunted walk, thinking about the female shape said to haunt it, when her mother appears.
That's not coincidence — it's the novel's metaphorical system in perfect alignment.
The legend of the Ghost's Walk, which we've been carrying since that first Lincolnshire chapter, is about a woman whose secret brought ruin on the family.
And here she is — that woman — walking toward her daughter.

What's remarkable is that we also get the information about what has been happening around Lady Dedlock — the letters, the campaign of accusation — and those scenes have an entirely different texture.
Bucket is practically gleeful when he reveals what Mrs. Bucket has been up to.
The pacing of that speech — it's almost musical.
He thunders through the evidence, and there at the centre of it, three words:
"Lady Dedlock, Murderess."
Dickens puts that in italics, and every time I read it aloud, I feel the shock of it fresh — even knowing what comes.
Because it's a lie — and it's also, in the world's terms, exactly what the world would say of her.
The accusation is false in its specifics and devastatingly true in its social logic.
And that, perhaps, is the final tragedy of Lady Dedlock — that even when the accusation is wrong, the exposure is real.
Her secret doesn't have to be murder to destroy her.
It only has to be known.
We'll return after the break to follow what happens when she finally runs — and what it costs her.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great sprawling masterpiece apart — and tries to explain why it still feels so urgently alive.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's most distinctive qualities: the way Dickens holds comedy and darkness in the same hand — sometimes in the same sentence.
Joining me are three exceptional readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Bleak House as an architect reads a cathedral — for the structure behind the beauty.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive, and he approaches the novel the way Dickens wrote it — for the voice, for the room, for the pleasure of performance.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite recovered — in the best possible sense.
Our question today is deceptively simple: how does Dickens make us laugh and break our hearts — and why does the combination feel like truth?
I think the place to start is with the house itself — because the name "Bleak House" is almost a trap that Dickens sets for the reader.
You arrive expecting bleakness, and what Esther actually describes is this gloriously, almost comically cluttered warmth.
Listen to this passage from Chapter Six, where she describes the rooms for the first time.

"Ada's sleeping-room was all flowers — in chintz and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool for greater state, on either side of the fire-place."
That phrase — "a little page of a stool for greater state" — is pure comic invention, but it's warm comedy.
The stool is playing at being important, and there's something genuinely tender in noticing that.
And then Dickens builds to this extraordinary closing sentence about their first impressions — which I'd call the architectural keystone of the whole passage.

"With its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House."
That sentence is structured like a piece of music — a series of "with" clauses building and building, and then the name lands at the end like a resolution.
And what I love about that sentence when you read it aloud is the rhythm of those "with" clauses — they do something almost physical to you.
You lean forward as a reader, as a listener, because Dickens keeps adding to the picture — and each addition is slightly unexpected.
"A hospitable jingle of preparations for dinner" — that word "jingle" is doing so much work.
It's comic, it's warm, and it's synesthetic — you hear the house before you see it.
But the darkness is never far away in this novel — and Dickens introduces it through Krook, the rag and bottle man, in one of the strangest little scenes in the book.
Esther has just seen the words "Jarndyce" and then "Bleak House" written and rubbed out by this mysterious, illiterate old man.

"When I told him, he laughed. In the same odd way, yet with the same rapidity, he then produced singly, and rubbed out singly, the letters forming the words Bleak House. These, in some astonishment, I also read; and he laughed again."
"He laughed again" — three words, and they're somehow the most sinister three words in that chapter.
Because it's not explained. The laugh sits there on the page, and you don't know whether to find it funny or frightening.
That ambiguity is what gets me every time I re-read that scene.

Krook laughs, but Esther doesn't know why, and neither do we — and yet Dickens has already placed those two words, "Jarndyce" and "Bleak House," together in a way that feels like a key turning in a lock.
You feel it before you understand it. That's a very specific and very powerful kind of writing.
And what strikes me is that the comedy and the menace are actually inseparable in Krook — his oddness is both grotesque and funny.
There's a structural counterpoint I keep coming back to, between that unsettling Krook scene and the much later moment when Bleak House finally becomes what its name seemed to deny.
In Chapter Sixty-Four, Jarndyce gives the house to Esther — and to Woodcourt — and the speech he makes is one of the most emotionally charged moments in the novel.
What's remarkable is how Dickens loads even this moment with darkness — the deaths of Esther's parents — before lifting into the gift.

"My dearest, Allan Woodcourt stood beside your father when he lay dead — stood beside your mother. This is Bleak House. This day I give this house its little mistress; and before God, it is the brightest day in all my life!"
That repetition — "stood beside your father... stood beside your mother" — is a kind of elegiac drumbeat.
And then "This is Bleak House" — just four words, almost a declaration, after everything the name has meant in the novel.
When I record that speech, I always have to pause before "This is Bleak House" — because the sentence is so naked, so stripped of Dickensian ornamentation.
After all the comic machinery of the Smallweeds and the court gossip and the Harmonic nights at the Sol — and there is glorious comedy there — Dickens can reach for something this direct.

Speaking of the Smallweed business — that passage in Chapter Thirty-Nine about the court's obsession with the rag and bottle shop is, I think, one of the funniest sustained passages Dickens ever wrote.
Dickens sets it up with this magnificent opening line.
"Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop."
"Fortunatus' purse" — an inexhaustible purse from fairy tale — and gossip is its treasure.
And then he just catalogues the delirious fantasies of the court: guineas pouring out of teapots, crown-pieces overflowing punch-bowls, mattresses stuffed with Bank of England notes.
It's communal madness rendered as pure farce — and it's brilliant precisely because the actual secret hidden in Krook's shop is anything but funny.
That contrast is what I find so devastating about the novel as a whole.
The comedy isn't a relief from the darkness — it's woven into it, so that when the darkness arrives, it's all the more shocking.
And Esther herself — this wonderfully self-deprecating, quietly determined narrator — carries this tension within her own voice.
There's a small, perfect moment in Chapter Forty-Four where she's talking to herself in the mirror — instructing herself to be cheerful.
"When you are mistress of Bleak House, you are to be as cheerful as a bird. In fact, you are always to be cheerful; so let us begin for once and for all."
That "for once and for all" breaks my heart every time.
Because cheerfulness, for Esther, is an act of will, not a natural state — and Dickens lets you see the effort behind it.
That's the great craft secret of Esther as a narrator, isn't it?
She is funny — genuinely funny, in a dry, self-aware way — but the comedy is never at the expense of her interiority.
Dickens gives her this habit of performing composure while the text quietly shows us the cracks in the performance.
And that dual movement — the composed surface, the revealed depth — is the novel's tonal signature in miniature.
What strikes me, hearing all three of you, is that the word "Bleak House" itself performs this double movement — it promises darkness and delivers something far more complex.
The house is warm, the name is cold — and Dickens never fully resolves that tension; he lets it stand as the novel's central irony.
We'll return after the break to look at how Dickens uses his comic grotesques — Krook, Smallweed, Chadband — to keep that darkness close to the surface, even in his funniest scenes.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we slow down and really listen to what Dickens is doing.
Today's segment is called The Unravelling — a moment in the novel where consequences begin to gather and the texture of Dickens's moral world comes sharply into focus.
We have three wonderful readers with us — and I want to give each of them a proper introduction.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is extraordinary at showing us how Dickens builds his effects — the architecture underneath the magic.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive, and he hears the prose the way a musician hears a score — for its rhythm, its timing, its performance potential.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager — she reads with both rigour and deep affection, and she will tell you plainly when a character deserves better.
Let's begin with Harold Skimpole — that great, gleaming enigma at the heart of the novel's moral comedy.
Skimpole is one of Dickens's most wicked creations, and I mean wicked in both senses of the word.
He is a moral criminal dressed up as a charming child — and the charm is so convincing that even Esther can barely get a grip on what's wrong.
What Dickens gives us in this early passage is something technically astonishing — Skimpole speaking of himself in the third person.
As if Skimpole were not at all his own affair.
He knew that Skimpole had his singularities but still had his claims too, which were the general business of the community and must not be slighted.
The community must not slight Harold Skimpole's claims — his claims on other people's money, other people's time, other people's conscience.
It is the most elegant confidence trick in Victorian fiction.
And what makes it so devastating, I think, is that Esther herself cannot quite name the problem.
Dickens writes her uncertainty with such precision — she doesn't say Skimpole is wrong.
She says she cannot reconcile what he says with her own sense of duty.
She was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them.
That conditional — she was confused by not understanding why — is one of the most quietly devastating phrases in the book.
Because Esther's confusion is also the reader's confusion — we are meant to feel the seductiveness before we feel the wrongness.
Dickens is building the trap slowly, and Esther is both the bait and the witness.
What strikes me every time I re-read it is that final sentence of the passage.
That he WAS free of them, I scarcely doubted; he was so very clear about it himself.
Dickens actually capitalises the WAS — in the original text — and that is not an accident.
It's Esther's own irony surfacing, almost against her will.
She cannot accuse him — her generosity won't allow it — but that capitalised WAS is her conscience speaking.
I find that one of the most moving technical choices in the whole novel.
And then he does it again — later, when Skimpole is at his most elaborately self-congratulatory.
By chapter thirty-one, Skimpole has refined his philosophy into something almost magnificent in its audacity.
He's been toasting Jo — this wretched crossing-sweeper boy — and imagining him as a future Lord Mayor of London.
And then, in the same breath, he turns back to himself.
What Harold Skimpole was, Harold Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he first made his own acquaintance.
He had accepted himself with all his failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the bargain.
Sound philosophy — I want to dwell on those two words.
Sound philosophy is what Skimpole calls a lifetime of cheerful parasitism, cloaked in the language of self-knowledge.
When I read that line aloud in the recording studio I had to stop and laugh — and then feel slightly sick.
That phrase — made his own acquaintance — is extraordinary.
It's the language of social introduction — as if he met himself at a party and found him delightful.
Dickens uses the conventions of politeness as a scalpel here.
The form of self-knowledge Skimpole displays is real — he does know himself — but he has severed knowledge from accountability.
And that, structurally, is what Dickens is doing across these two passages — showing us how a man can be radically self-aware and utterly without conscience simultaneously.
It is one of the novel's great moral insights — and it's delivered through comedy, which makes it land harder.
Let's turn to the women on the periphery of this moral world — and they are not always where you'd expect to find them.
Eleanor, you've been thinking about Mrs. Pardiggle — another kind of moral impostor, though a very different one from Skimpole.
Mrs. Pardiggle is extraordinary precisely because she is the mirror image of Skimpole — where he refuses all duty, she performs an excess of it.
And yet Dickens places them on the same moral level — both are using a public role to avoid being genuinely present to other people.
The description of her arrival is almost slapstick, but it does real work.
She was a formidable style of lady with spectacles, a prominent nose, and a loud voice, who had the effect of wanting a great deal of room.
Wanting a great deal of room — that is the whole character in five words.
She literally takes up space — she knocks over chairs with her skirts — but the real space she's occupying is other people's moral agency.
Her charity leaves no room for the charitable instincts of anyone else.
She seemed to come in like cold weather — and to make the little Pardiggles blue as they followed.
The little Pardiggles blue — there's something almost cruel in the comedy of that image.
Those children are blue — chilled — by their own mother's performance of virtue.
It is a single image that indicts an entire system of philanthropic self-congratulation.
And Dickens puts it in — almost in passing — in a subordinate clause.
What I love is that Esther and Ada receive her timidly — that's the word Dickens uses.
Two intelligent, kind women — reduced to timidity by someone whose whole project is supposedly to help people.
The comedy is also a kind of horror — this is what aggressive virtue does to the room it enters.
And Dickens trusts his metaphor to carry it — cold weather, blue children, knocked-over chairs.
He never editorialises directly.
Caroline, you've been sitting with Mrs. Woodcourt — a quieter figure, but one who creates a very particular kind of discomfort for Esther.
Mrs. Woodcourt is, in a way, the most insidious figure in this cluster of passages — because she is genuinely kind.
She takes very kindly to Esther — Esther says so.
And yet she was extremely confidential — so much so that sometimes she almost made me uncomfortable.
That word — uncomfortable — is doing so much work in such a small space.
Esther immediately corrects herself — I had no right, I knew very well, to be uncomfortable — and that self-correction is the wound.
Mrs. Woodcourt is manoeuvring around Esther's future — around her son Allan's attachment — with smiling, plausible, suffocating attention.
And Esther, who cannot assert her own right to feel what she feels, absorbs it all and apologises to herself for minding.
That structure — feeling something, then doubting your right to feel it — is Esther's signature move, and it is heartbreaking every single time.
Dickens has built a narrator who is so thoroughly educated into self-erasure that she cannot even trust her own discomfort.
With all I could do, I could not quite help it — that trailing qualifier is everything.
She resists her own response.
She manages not quite to suppress it.
And that not quite is where the reader's heart lives — in that tiny gap of honesty.
Reading Esther aloud, you learn very quickly that those qualifiers are the performance instructions.
Every I am far from sure of, every I could not quite help it — these are the places where you slow down and let the silence speak.
Because Dickens is writing a character who is always editing herself in real time — and if you rush past those moments, you lose the whole person.
She is the most technically demanding narrator I've ever performed.
We have covered a great deal of moral ground today — Skimpole's charming amorality, Mrs. Pardiggle's bullying virtue, Mrs. Woodcourt's smiling pressure on Esther's sense of self.

What strikes me, pulling these passages together, is how Dickens distributes moral failure across the full social spectrum — it is not class that determines it, but a particular severing of action from genuine human attention.
Our three readers have made that visible — and audible — in ways that I think Dickens himself would have recognised as the highest form of homage.
We'll be back very soon with another segment of Bleak House Unpacked.
We've arrived at our final segment — and what a place to end.
The closing chapters of Bleak House are remarkable for the way Dickens refuses easy consolation.
There is joy, genuine and hard-won joy — but also ruin, and grief that doesn't fully resolve.
Caroline Woodcourt has been our most intimate reader throughout this episode — attentive to feeling, to music, to what it costs us as readers.
Caroline, the closing movement belongs to you.
Thank you — and I want to start where the novel earns its happiness most carefully, which is with Jarndyce's great speech to Esther in chapter sixty-four.
He has been carrying this secret — Esther's love for Woodcourt, Woodcourt's love for Esther — and instead of suppressing it, he has built a whole new life around it for her.
And then he reports what he actually said to Mrs. Woodcourt — this extraordinary challenge about pedigree and legitimacy.

'Come you, and see my child from hour to hour; set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this — and tell me what is the true legitimacy when you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject.'
He scorned to mince it — that's the phrase that stops me every time.
Jarndyce doesn't soften Esther's illegitimacy — he lays it out in full, and then asks what it actually means, set against everything she is.
What I love about that speech is its structural audacity — Jarndyce essentially performs a cross-examination inside a tender scene.
The novel has been soaked in legal language from the first page, and here Jarndyce turns that language against the class prejudice that has damaged Esther her entire life.
'The true legitimacy' — he's appropriating the vocabulary of inheritance law and asking it to mean something human instead.
And then the exclamation — 'honour to her old Welsh blood, my dear!'
'I believe the heart it animates beats no less warmly, no less admiringly, no less lovingly, towards Dame Durden than my own!'
That triple 'no less' — it's almost legal testimony, almost an oath.
Dickens is writing Jarndyce's emotional climax in the syntax of a closing argument.
And when you read it aloud — which I have done, rather more than once — there's something almost breathless in how Dickens paces that revelation.
He keeps interrupting himself: 'Hush, little woman! Don't cry; this is to be a day of joy.'
'I have looked forward to it — for months on months!'
The dashes do something wonderful there — they mimic a man barely containing his own excitement.
Jarndyce has been so carefully, painfully restrained for three-quarters of this novel.
And now he gets to let it out — and Dickens gives him these gorgeous, lurching interruptions to show us exactly that release.
There's also this quiet little thread running through these chapters — the 'Dame Durden' refrain.
Jarndyce asks, earlier in the same chapter, what a Dame Durden it is to read a face.
'No; have you really, my dear? What a Dame Durden it is to read a face!'
It's a tiny moment — comic, affectionate — but it reminds you that Esther has been watching everyone around her with extraordinary attentiveness throughout.
And that Jarndyce sees her doing it, and loves her for it.
Can we hold the joy for a moment and acknowledge what coexists with it?
Because Dickens doesn't let the closing movement be simply triumphant.
Richard is dead, the Jarndyce suit has consumed its only prize — its own costs — and Chancery grinds on, essentially unchanged.
The novel insists that personal happiness and systemic ruin can exist simultaneously — they don't cancel each other out.
That double vision is what makes the ending feel true rather than sentimental.
And then — almost as if Dickens needs to breathe — you get Turveydrop.
Even in these closing pages, even with everything that hangs over the novel, Dickens cannot resist Turveydrop performing his magnificent, boundless generosity — at absolutely no cost to himself.
The speech is a masterpiece of comic hypocrisy dressed as deportment.
'Do not even allow my simple requirements to be considered if they should at any time interfere with your own, my Caroline. Your necessities are greater than mine.'
The sheer grandeur of the self-sacrifice he's performing while sacrificing absolutely nothing.
It's hilarious, and it's also a little bit chilling — Caddy will be managing that man until one of them dies.
That's exactly it — Dickens is honest about what doesn't change.
Turveydrop survives. Chancery survives. Mrs. Jellyby will find a new cause.
And yet Esther has her house, her children, her Woodcourt — and Jarndyce, rather wonderfully, has made peace with all of it.
The novel ends in a kind of earned, incomplete happiness — which is, I think, the only kind worth writing about.
Earned and incomplete — I think that's the most honest description of this novel's ending I've heard.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — it has been a genuine pleasure thinking alongside all three of you today.
Bleak House remains one of the most extraordinary things the English novel has ever done — a book about fog and delay and death that is somehow also about the persistence of human warmth.
If this conversation has sent you back to the novel — or sent you to it for the first time — then we have done our work.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.

My Lady Dedlock has returned to her house in town for a few days
previous to her departure for Paris, where her ladyship intends to
stay some weeks, after which her movements are uncertain. The
fashionable intelligence says so for the comfort of the Parisians,
and it knows all fashionable things. To know things otherwise were to
be unfashionable. My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in
familiar conversation, her “place” in Lincolnshire. The waters are
out in Lincolnshire. An arch of the bridge in the park has been
sapped and sopped away. The adjacent low-lying ground for half a mile
in breadth is a stagnant river with melancholy trees for islands in
it and a surface punctured all over, all day long, with falling rain.
My Lady Dedlock’s place has been extremely dreary. The weather for
many a day and night has been so wet that the trees seem wet through,
and the soft loppings and prunings of the woodman’s axe can make no
crash or crackle as they fall. The deer, looking soaked, leave
quagmires where they pass. The shot of a rifle loses its sharpness in
the moist air, and its smoke moves in a tardy little cloud towards
the green rise, coppice-topped, that makes a background for the
falling rain. The view from my Lady Dedlock’s own windows is
alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink. The vases
on the stone terrace in the foreground catch the rain all day; and
the heavy drops fall—drip, drip, drip—upon the broad flagged
pavement, called from old time the Ghost’s Walk, all night. On
Sundays the little church in the park is mouldy; the oaken pulpit
breaks out into a cold sweat; and there is a general smell and taste
as of the ancient Dedlocks in their graves. My Lady Dedlock (who is
childless), looking out in the early twilight from her boudoir at a
keeper’s lodge and seeing the light of a fire upon the latticed
panes, and smoke rising from the chimney, and a child, chased by a
woman, running out into the rain to meet the shining figure of a
wrapped-up man coming through the gate, has been put quite out of
temper. My Lady Dedlock says she has been “bored to death.”
c2:p2.summary: Lady Dedlock returns to her Lincolnshire estate before departing for Paris, where the landscape is depicted as relentlessly dreary and sodden; her observation of a family scene at a keeper's lodge disrupts her usual composure.

c48:p105.text:
For a little while they are silent. Lady Dedlock has eaten no dinner,
but has twice or thrice poured out water with a steady hand and drunk
it. She rises from table, takes a lounging-chair, and reclines in it,
shading her face. There is nothing in her manner to express weakness
or excite compassion. It is thoughtful, gloomy, concentrated. “This
woman,” thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark
object closing up her view, “is a study.”
c48:p105.summary: In the silence that follows, Lady Dedlock maintains thoughtful composure while remaining emotionally turbulent; Tulkinghorn regards her as a fascinating psychological study.
c48:p105.best_quote: This woman,' thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view, 'is a study.'

c36:p18.text:
I was resting at my favourite point after a long ramble, and Charley
was gathering violets at a little distance from me. I had been
looking at the Ghost’s Walk lying in a deep shade of masonry afar off
and picturing to myself the female shape that was said to haunt it
when I became aware of a figure approaching through the wood. The
perspective was so long and so darkened by leaves, and the shadows of
the branches on the ground made it so much more intricate to the eye,
that at first I could not discern what figure it was. By little and
little it revealed itself to be a woman’s—a lady’s—Lady Dedlock’s.
She was alone and coming to where I sat with a much quicker step, I
observed to my surprise, than was usual with her.
c36:p18.summary: As Esther rests at her favorite spot, a woman emerges through the wood—Lady Dedlock, approaching with unusual haste and emotion.

c54:p134.text:
“And she got encouragement in it from hearing that I was always here,
which was done a-purpose. Now, open that pocket-book of mine, Sir
Leicester Dedlock, if I may take the liberty of throwing it towards
you, and look at the letters sent to me, each with the two words
‘Lady Dedlock’ in it. Open the one directed to yourself, which I
stopped this very morning, and read the three words ‘Lady Dedlock,
Murderess’ in it. These letters have been falling about like a shower
of lady-birds. What do you say now to Mrs. Bucket, from her spy-place
having seen them all written by this young woman? What do you say to
Mrs. Bucket having, within this half-hour, secured the corresponding
ink and paper, fellow half-sheets and what not? What do you say to
Mrs. Bucket having watched the posting of ’em every one by this young
woman, Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet?” Mr. Bucket asks, triumphant
in his admiration of his lady’s genius.
c54:p134.summary: Bucket reveals that Hortense sent multiple letters accusing Lady Dedlock of murder, which Mrs. Bucket observed being written and collected as evidence.

c6:p46.text:
The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.
c6:p46.summary: Detailed description of Bleak House's furnishings in each room, establishing a warm, hospitable environment filled with quirky collections and careful comfort.
c6:p46.best_quote: with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House

c5:p86.text:
When I told him, he laughed. In the same odd way, yet with the same
rapidity, he then produced singly, and rubbed out singly, the letters
forming the words Bleak House. These, in some astonishment, I also
read; and he laughed again.
c5:p86.summary: Esther reads both 'Jarndyce' and 'Bleak House' with astonishment; Krook laughs mysteriously.

c64:p37.text:
“One more last word. When Allan Woodcourt spoke to you, my dear, he
spoke with my knowledge and consent—but I gave him no encouragement,
not I, for these surprises were my great reward, and I was too
miserly to part with a scrap of it. He was to come and tell me all
that passed, and he did. I have no more to say. My dearest, Allan
Woodcourt stood beside your father when he lay dead—stood beside
your mother. This is Bleak House. This day I give this house its
little mistress; and before God, it is the brightest day in all my
life!”
c64:p37.summary: Jarndyce reveals that Woodcourt attended both Esther's parents at death; he formally gives Esther the house as the 'little mistress' of Bleak House and declares it the brightest day of his life.
c64:p37.best_quote: My dearest, Allan Woodcourt stood beside your father when he lay dead—stood beside your mother. This is Bleak House. This day I give this house its little mistress; and before God, it is the brightest day in all my life!

c39:p58.text:
Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus’ purse
of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop.
Regularly, every morning at eight, is the elder Mr. Smallweed brought
down to the corner and carried in, accompanied by Mrs. Smallweed,
Judy, and Bart; and regularly, all day, do they all remain there
until nine at night, solaced by gipsy dinners, not abundant in
quantity, from the cook’s shop, rummaging and searching, digging,
delving, and diving among the treasures of the late lamented. What
those treasures are they keep so secret that the court is maddened.
In its delirium it imagines guineas pouring out of tea-pots,
crown-pieces overflowing punch-bowls, old chairs and mattresses
stuffed with Bank of England notes. It possesses itself of the
sixpenny history (with highly coloured folding frontispiece) of Mr.
Daniel Dancer and his sister, and also of Mr. Elwes, of Suffolk, and
transfers all the facts from those authentic narratives to Mr. Krook.
Twice when the dustman is called in to carry off a cartload of old
paper, ashes, and broken bottles, the whole court assembles and pries
into the baskets as they come forth. Many times the two gentlemen who
write with the ravenous little pens on the tissue-paper are seen
prowling in the neighbourhood—shy of each other, their late
partnership being dissolved. The Sol skilfully carries a vein of the
prevailing interest through the Harmonic nights. Little Swills, in
what are professionally known as “patter” allusions to the subject,
is received with loud applause; and the same vocalist “gags” in the
regular business like a man inspired. Even Miss M. Melvilleson, in
the revived Caledonian melody of “We’re a-Nodding,” points the
sentiment that “the dogs love broo” (whatever the nature of that
refreshment may be) with such archness and such a turn of the head
towards next door that she is immediately understood to mean Mr.
Smallweed loves to find money, and is nightly honoured with a double
encore. For all this, the court discovers nothing; and as Mrs. Piper
and Mrs. Perkins now communicate to the late lodger whose appearance
is the signal for a general rally, it is in one continual ferment to
discover everything, and more.
c39:p58.summary: The entire court becomes obsessed with Smallweed's search through Krook's possessions, inventing elaborate fantasies about hidden treasure. The narrator describes daily routines and even entertainment at the local pub incorporating references to the search.
c39:p58.best_quote: Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop.

c44:p39.text:
“That is more like the composed look you comforted me with, my dear,
when you showed me such a change!” said I, beginning to let down my
hair. “When you are mistress of Bleak House, you are to be as
cheerful as a bird. In fact, you are always to be cheerful; so let us
begin for once and for all.”
c44:p39.summary: Esther encourages herself to adopt a cheerful demeanor befitting the future mistress of Bleak House, undertaking to be always bright and positive.
c44:p39.best_quote: When you are mistress of Bleak House, you are to be as cheerful as a bird. In fact, you are always to be cheerful; so let us begin for once and for all.

c6:p68.text:
All this and a great deal more he told us, not only with the utmost
brilliancy and enjoyment, but with a certain vivacious
candour—speaking of himself as if he were not at all his own affair,
as if Skimpole were a third person, as if he knew that Skimpole had
his singularities but still had his claims too, which were the
general business of the community and must not be slighted. He was
quite enchanting. If I felt at all confused at that early time in
endeavouring to reconcile anything he said with anything I had
thought about the duties and accountabilities of life (which I am far
from sure of), I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was
free of them. That he WAS free of them, I scarcely doubted; he was so
very clear about it himself.
c6:p68.summary: Esther observes Skimpole's extraordinary candor and charm while noting her confusion about why society seems to excuse him from ordinary moral obligations.
c6:p68.best_quote: If I felt at all confused at that early time in endeavouring to reconcile anything he said with anything I had thought about the duties and accountabilities of life...I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them

c31:p92.text:
He was extremely gay all the rest of the evening, for he absolutely
chirped—those were his delighted words—when he thought by what a
happy talent for business he was surrounded. He gave us, in his glass
of negus, “Better health to our young friend!” and supposed and gaily
pursued the case of his being reserved like Whittington to become
Lord Mayor of London. In that event, no doubt, he would establish the
Jarndyce Institution and the Summerson Almshouses, and a little
annual Corporation Pilgrimage to St. Albans. He had no doubt, he
said, that our young friend was an excellent boy in his way, but his
way was not the Harold Skimpole way; what Harold Skimpole was, Harold
Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he
first made his own acquaintance; he had accepted himself with all his
failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the
bargain; and he hoped we would do the same.
c31:p92.summary: Skimpole cheerfully pursues fanciful thoughts about Jo becoming Lord Mayor, then expounds his philosophy of self-acceptance without moral growth.
c31:p92.best_quote: what Harold Skimpole was, Harold Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he first made his own acquaintance; he had accepted himself with all his failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the bargain

c8:p53.text:
She was a formidable style of lady with spectacles, a prominent nose,
and a loud voice, who had the effect of wanting a great deal of room.
And she really did, for she knocked down little chairs with her
skirts that were quite a great way off. As only Ada and I were at
home, we received her timidly, for she seemed to come in like cold
weather and to make the little Pardiggles blue as they followed.
c8:p53.summary: Mrs. Pardiggle arrives with her five sons; she is imposing, loud, and physically dominating, and she makes Esther and Ada nervous as she literally knocks over furniture with her skirts.
c8:p53.best_quote: She was a formidable style of lady with spectacles, a prominent nose, and a loud voice, who had the effect of wanting a great deal of room.

c30:p0.text:
Richard had been gone away some time when a visitor came to pass a
few days with us. It was an elderly lady. It was Mrs. Woodcourt, who,
having come from Wales to stay with Mrs. Bayham Badger and having
written to my guardian, “by her son Allan’s desire,” to report that
she had heard from him and that he was well “and sent his kind
remembrances to all of us,” had been invited by my guardian to make a
visit to Bleak House. She stayed with us nearly three weeks. She took
very kindly to me and was extremely confidential, so much so that
sometimes she almost made me uncomfortable. I had no right, I knew
very well, to be uncomfortable because she confided in me, and I felt
it was unreasonable; still, with all I could do, I could not quite
help it.
c30:p0.summary: Mrs. Woodcourt, mother of Allan Woodcourt, arrives to stay at Bleak House after visiting Mrs. Badger, and Esther finds her confidential manner somewhat uncomfortable despite her kindness.

c64:p35.text:
“Hush, little woman! Don’t cry; this is to be a day of joy. I have
looked forward to it,” he said exultingly, “for months on months! A
few words more, Dame Trot, and I have said my say. Determined not to
throw away one atom of my Esther’s worth, I took Mrs. Woodcourt into
a separate confidence. ‘Now, madam,’ said I, ‘I clearly perceive—and
indeed I know, to boot—that your son loves my ward. I am further
very sure that my ward loves your son, but will sacrifice her love to
a sense of duty and affection, and will sacrifice it so completely,
so entirely, so religiously, that you should never suspect it though
you watched her night and day.’ Then I told her all our
story—ours—yours and mine. ‘Now, madam,’ said I, ‘come you, knowing
this, and live with us. Come you, and see my child from hour to hour;
set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this’—for
I scorned to mince it—‘and tell me what is the true legitimacy when
you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject.’ Why, honour
to her old Welsh blood, my dear,” cried my guardian with enthusiasm,
“I believe the heart it animates beats no less warmly, no less
admiringly, no less lovingly, towards Dame Durden than my own!”
c64:p35.summary: Jarndyce explains how he told Mrs. Woodcourt of Esther and Woodcourt's love, challenged her prejudices about pedigree, and ultimately convinced her to see Esther's true worth and character.
c64:p35.best_quote: 'Now, madam,' said I, 'come you, knowing this, and live with us. Come you, and see my child from hour to hour; set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this'—for I scorned to mince it—'and tell me what is the true legitimacy when you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject.'

c64:p16.text:
“No; have you really, my dear?” said he. “What a Dame Durden it is to
read a face!”
c64:p16.summary: Jarndyce playfully asks what a 'Dame Durden' it is to read a face.

c50:p32.text:
“Charming! We must take care of our dear Caroline, Miss Summerson. We
must spare nothing that will restore her. We must nourish her. My
dear Caroline”—he would turn to his daughter-in-law with infinite
generosity and protection—“want for nothing, my love. Frame a wish
and gratify it, my daughter. Everything this house contains,
everything my room contains, is at your service, my dear. Do not,” he
would sometimes add in a burst of deportment, “even allow my simple
requirements to be considered if they should at any time interfere
with your own, my Caroline. Your necessities are greater than mine.”
c50:p32.summary: Mr. Turveydrop addresses Caddy with exaggerated generosity, offering everything the house contains while framing his own needs as secondary, all delivered with theatrical grace.
c50:p32.best_quote: Do not, he would sometimes add in a burst of deportment, even allow my simple requirements to be considered if they should at any time interfere with your own, my Caroline. Your necessities are greater than mine.
